source.name: Eurostat nrg_inf_epcrw (Solar photovoltaic, net maximum electrical capacity)

trend_full.method: Theil-Sen slope + Gilbert 95% CI; Mann-Kendall (ties-corrected), Hamed-Rao variance correction

trend_recent.method: Theil-Sen slope + Gilbert 95% CI; Mann-Kendall (ties-corrected), no autocorrelation correction needed

added_mw_trend.method: Theil-Sen slope + Gilbert 95% CI; Mann-Kendall (ties-corrected), no autocorrelation correction needed

en.headline: Spain had about 36 GW of solar panels (photovoltaic) installed at the end of 2024, 8 times more than in 2015.
en.growth: Since 2019 the installed amount has grown about 32% per year, so it doubles roughly every 2.5 years. In 2024 alone about 6.2 GW of new panels were added. New additions per year are also clearly increasing since 2015.
en.rank: In 2024 Spain was 2nd of the 27 EU countries in installed solar panels, after Germany, with about 12% of the EU total.

es.headline: España tenía unos 36 GW de paneles solares (fotovoltaicos) instalados a finales de 2024, 8 veces más que en 2015.
es.growth: Desde 2019 la potencia instalada ha crecido alrededor de un 32% al año, así que se duplica cada 2,5 años aproximadamente. Solo en 2024 se añadieron unos 6,2 GW nuevos. Lo que se instala cada año también aumenta claramente desde 2015.
es.rank: En 2024 España era el país número 2 de los 27 de la UE en paneles solares instalados, detrás de Alemania, con cerca del 12% del total de la UE.

notes: Capacity is not generation: MW is the maximum power the installed panels can deliver, not the electricity (MWh) they actually produced.

Cumulative capacity is a running total that almost never goes down, so a significant upward trend on it is close to mechanical; the more informative test is the trend of annual additions (added_mw_trend).
added_mw is the year-on-year difference of net capacity; it can understate gross new builds when old plants are retired or re-rated.
Net maximum electrical capacity (Eurostat CAP_NET_ELC, total). Eurostat also publishes AC and DC sub-series; they are not mixed here.

Trends: Theil-Sen slope with Gilbert 95% CI and Mann-Kendall test (packages/science/trends.py), Hamed-Rao autocorrelation correction when lag-1 autocorrelation is significant. Smooth growth curves are strongly autocorrelated, so p-values are indicative.
EU ranking uses the latest year (2024) for which all 27 EU countries report a value.

This is national context for the screening: the featured Jaén–Granada cell is about where new plants fit; this series shows how fast Spain is building them. The GEM plant registry cannot give a yearly trend (docs/PV_HISTORY.md), so official statistics are used here.
Annual additions are lumpy (e.g. the 2008 tariff rush, 2015-2018 near zero, a 2022 peak), so their positive trend since 2015 mainly says the market restarted after 2018; it is not a forecast.
Spain and the 3rd country are close in 2024 (ES 35.8 GW vs IT 35.4 GW); the 2nd place is not a large margin.
Eurostat data are official statistics; the trend analysis is ours.
